what_it_does: Processing-in-memory (PIM) chips do math directly inside the memory array instead of shipping data to a separate processor — this is more energy-efficient, but it means thousands of tiny circuits switch on and off simultaneously, causing a voltage sag called IR-drop. On a real commercial 7nm chip running at 256 trillion operations per second, this sag hit 140 millivolts, which risks incorrect computation and chip failure. This paper, AIM, solves that problem at the software and hardware level together: it teaches the AI model stored on the chip to use weight values that inherently cause less voltage sag, and pairs that with a hardware monitor that dynamically adjusts the chip's voltage and clock speed based on how bad the sag actually is at runtime.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Every weight value stored in a PIM chip's memory has a binary representation (a pattern of 1s and 0s). As the chip multiplies inputs through those weights, each weight bit that equals '1' causes a tiny electrical switching event. More 1-bits switching at once means more current spike, which means more voltage sag (IR-drop). The chip is normally designed to tolerate the absolute worst case — every cell switching at once — but real AI workloads never come close to that. This gap is the optimization opportunity.

Metrics first. AIM introduces two measurements. Rtog is the fraction of bits that actually toggle each clock cycle — the real-time sag indicator, but hard to precompute. HR (Hamming Rate) is simply the fraction of '1' bits in the stored weights — a static property that upper-bounds Rtog and can be optimized before deployment.

Software optimizations (offline). LHR (Lower Hamming Rate) adds a penalty term during the model's training-with-integer-weights phase (called quantization-aware training). The penalty pushes weight values toward integers that have few 1-bits in binary, like 0 and 8. The gradient of this penalty is computed via smooth interpolation, making it compatible with standard gradient-based training. WDS (Weight Distribution Shift) adds a constant offset delta (e.g., 8) to all weights before loading them onto the chip, shifting the distribution toward positive small integers — which have fewer 1-bits than negative numbers in two's complement encoding. A tiny hardware compensator next to each memory bank subtracts the mathematical error this introduces, pipelined so it doesn't slow anything down.

Hardware adjustment (runtime). IR-Booster extends traditional voltage-frequency scaling by adding HR-aware operating points. Instead of always using the worst-case voltage/frequency setting, it pre-selects a safe level based on precomputed HR bounds, then aggressively tries a lower-voltage or higher-frequency setting. A ring-oscillator-based voltage sensor detects when the supply drops dangerously low and signals an IRFailure; the chip then recomputes the affected cycle and dials back slightly. Over time, the system learns the right operating point for each workload segment.

The result. Post-layout simulation on a real 7nm 256-TOPS chip shows up to 69.2% reduction in IR-drop, translating to 2.29x better energy efficiency or 1.15x higher throughput, with no accuracy loss.
